question: Article 40 of the Indian constitution, "Organisation of village panchayats", is a ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Directive Principles of State Policy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 40 falls in Part IV (Articles 36–51) of the Constitution, which contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). (राज्य के नीति निदेशक तत्व)

• It directs the State to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government.

• DPSPs are borrowed from the Irish Constitution and are non-justiciable — they cannot be enforced in a court of law, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country.

• Article 40 was given practical shape by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which inserted Part IX (Articles 243–243O) on Panchayats.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A (Part IVA), added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12–35) and are justiciable, enforceable under Article 32.

• A legal right is one created by ordinary statute, not by the Constitution.

NOTE

• Other Gandhian DPSPs: Art. 43 (cottage industries), Art. 46 (promotion of SC/ST interests), Art. 47 (prohibition of intoxicating drinks), Art. 48 (cow slaughter ban).

• Art. 44 — Uniform Civil Code; Art. 45 — early childhood care; Art. 50 — separation of judiciary from executive.

question: The day to day condition of the atmosphere at a place with respect to the temperature humidity, rainfall, wind speed etc. is called ______ at that place.
solution_text:
The correct answer is weather.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Weather is the day-to-day (short-term) state of the atmosphere at a place with respect to temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed and direction, cloudiness, etc. (मौसम)

• Weather can change within hours or even minutes; it is studied by meteorology.

• The element of weather that changes most during a day is temperature; the maximum temperature usually occurs in the afternoon and the minimum in the early morning.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Climate is the average weather pattern of a place taken over a long period (about 30 years or more). (जलवायु)

• Environment means the total surroundings — biotic and abiotic — in which an organism lives.

• Ecology is the branch of biology dealing with the relationship of organisms with one another and with their surroundings; the term was coined by Ernst Haeckel.

NOTE

• Instruments: Thermometer — temperature; Barometer — atmospheric pressure; Hygrometer — humidity; Anemometer — wind speed; Rain gauge — rainfall.

• The India Meteorological Department (IMD), set up in 1875, is headquartered in New Delhi.

question: The disease-causing microbes are called ________ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is pathogens.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pathogens are disease-causing micro-organisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths. (रोगजनक)

• Examples: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB), Plasmodium (malaria), Vibrio cholerae (cholera), Varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox).

• Diseases spread by pathogens are called communicable/infectious diseases; they spread through air, water, food, physical contact or vectors.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Toxins are poisonous substances produced by organisms (e.g., the toxin of *Clostridium tetani* causing tetanus); they are not themselves microbes.

• Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients into the soil — they are useful, not disease-causing.

• Antibodies are Y-shaped immunoglobulin proteins produced by B-lymphocytes that fight antigens; they defend the body against pathogens.

NOTE

• Vector-borne diseases: female *Anopheles* mosquito — malaria; *Aedes aegypti* — dengue, chikungunya, zika; housefly — typhoid, cholera.

• Louis Pasteur proposed the germ theory of disease; Robert Koch discovered the TB and cholera bacteria.

question: The substances which reduce friction are called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is lubricants.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Substances applied between two surfaces in contact to reduce friction are called lubricants. (स्नेहक)

• Common lubricants: grease, oil, graphite (used in dry form for machine parts). A thin layer of lubricant forms a film between the surfaces so that they do not directly rub against each other.

• Friction is the force that opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact; it is greater on rough surfaces and less on smooth surfaces.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Fluids (liquids and gases) exert drag/fluid friction; objects moving through them are given a streamlined shape to reduce it.

• Magnets attract magnetic materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel; they have nothing to do with reducing friction.

• Springs store elastic potential energy and obey Hooke's law (F = kx).

NOTE

• Order of magnitude: Static friction > Sliding (kinetic) friction > Rolling friction. This is why ball bearings are used in machines.

• Friction is a necessary evil — it helps us walk, write and brake, but it causes wear and tear and loss of energy as heat.

question: In 1927, B.R Ambedkar started which movement with Dalits?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Temple entry movement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Dr. B. R. Ambedkar led the struggle of the Dalits for the right to use public water sources and to enter Hindu temples, launching the Mahad Satyagraha at the Chavdar tank, Mahad (Maharashtra) in March 1927. (मंदिर प्रवेश आंदोलन)

• At Mahad on 25 December 1927 he publicly burnt the Manusmriti as a protest against caste discrimination.

• He founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) and started the journals Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Bharat (1927).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Self-Respect Movement was started in 1925 in Tamil Nadu by E. V. Ramasamy 'Periyar', not by Ambedkar.

• Ambedkar signed the Poona Pact (1932) with Mahatma Gandhi, replacing separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats.

• He was Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly and India's first Law Minister; awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1990 (posthumously).

NOTE

• Ambedkar's famous Kalaram Temple entry Satyagraha was launched at Nashik in 1930; some sources therefore date the temple-entry agitation to 1930, but the movement began with the Mahad Satyagraha of 1927.

• Related: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25, Kerala) for temple-road entry; Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931) led by K. Kelappan.

question: "Solung" is a festival celebrated by the Adi Tribe of which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arunachal Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Solung is an agricultural festival celebrated by the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, generally in the first week of September for about five days. (सोलुंग)

• It is celebrated after the sowing of seeds, praying for a bumper harvest and the prosperity of men and cattle.

• A special feature is the Ponung dance performed by women, and the making of Beyop — offerings of indigenous weapons hung in houses.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Other festivals of Arunachal Pradesh: Losar (Monpa), Mopin (Galo), Nyokum (Nyishi), Dree (Apatani), Si-Donyi (Tagin), Boori Boot (Hill Miri).

• Himachal Pradesh — Kullu Dussehra, Minjar Fair, Lavi Fair.

• Madhya Pradesh — Bhagoria festival of the Bhil tribe; Andhra Pradesh — Ugadi, Sankranti.

NOTE

• Arunachal Pradesh: capital Itanagar; became a full state on 20 February 1987; it is India's easternmost state and the sun rises first at Dong village.

• Major tribes: Adi, Nyishi, Apatani, Galo, Monpa, Mishmi, Tagin, Wancho, Nocte.

question: Which river flows between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Narmada.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Narmada flows westwards through a rift valley (trough) between the Vindhya range in the north and the Satpura range in the south. (नर्मदा)

• It rises from the Amarkantak plateau in Madhya Pradesh and falls into the Gulf of Khambhat (Arabian Sea) — length about 1,312 km, the longest west-flowing river of India.

• Famous features on it: the Marble Rocks and Dhuandhar Falls at Jabalpur, and the Sardar Sarovar Dam (Gujarat) and Indira Sagar Dam (MP).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Godavari — the largest peninsular river (Dakshina Ganga), rises at Trimbakeshwar, Nashik and drains into the Bay of Bengal.

• Son — a major right-bank tributary of the Ganga, also rising near Amarkantak.

• Mahanadi — rises in Chhattisgarh; the Hirakud Dam (Odisha), India's longest dam, is built on it.

NOTE

• The other major west-flowing peninsular river in a rift valley is the Tapi (Tapti), which flows between the Satpura and the Ajanta/Satmala hills.

• Narmada is the lifeline of Madhya Pradesh; the Narmada Bachao Andolan was led by Medha Patkar.

question: The Virupaksha Temple is situated at ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hampi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Virupaksha Temple is located at Hampi, on the bank of the Tungabhadra river in Bellary/Vijayanagara district, Karnataka. (विरुपाक्ष मंदिर)

• It is dedicated to Lord Shiva as Virupaksha (Pampapati), consort of the local goddess Pampa; it dates from the 7th century and was greatly expanded under the Vijayanagara rulers, notably Krishnadeva Raya.

• Hampi — Group of Monuments was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire (founded 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Surat (Gujarat) — an important port and diamond/textile city on the Tapi river.

• Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh) — famous for the Great Stupa built by Ashoka; a UNESCO site (1989).

• Jaipur (Rajasthan) — the Pink City, founded by Sawai Jai Singh II in 1727; a UNESCO site (2019).

NOTE

• Other Hampi monuments: Vittala Temple with the stone chariot and musical pillars, Hazara Rama Temple, Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables.

• Foreign travellers who visited Vijayanagara: Nicolo de Conti, Abdur Razzaq, Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz.

question: Which country is the second largest producer of crude steel in the world for FY 2020-21?
solution_text:
The correct answer is India.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India is the second largest producer of crude steel in the world, after China, a position it has held since 2018 when it overtook Japan. (कच्चा इस्पात)

• India is also the second largest consumer of finished steel and the largest producer of sponge iron/DRI (direct reduced iron) in the world.

• The Ministry of Steel administers the sector; the National Steel Policy 2017 targets 300 million tonnes of crude steel capacity by 2030–31.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• China is by far the largest producer of crude steel, accounting for over half of world output.

• Japan ranks third, followed by the USA and Russia.

• Australia is a leading exporter of iron ore and coal, not a top steel producer.

NOTE

• Major Indian steel plants: Bhilai (Chhattisgarh) — Russian aid; Rourkela (Odisha) — German aid; Durgapur (West Bengal) — British aid; Bokaro (Jharkhand) — Russian aid; Jamshedpur (TISCO, 1907) — India's first modern steel plant, set up by Jamsetji Tata.

• SAIL (Steel Authority of India Ltd) was set up in 1954/1973 and is a Maharatna PSU.

question: Which famous Indian musician is associated with musical instrument Santoor?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pandit Shiv Kumar Sharma.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pandit Shiv Kumar Sharma (1938–2022) was the maestro who established the Santoor, a hundred-stringed folk instrument of Kashmir, as a solo Hindustani classical concert instrument. (संतूर)

• The Santoor is a trapezoid-shaped stringed (tata vadya) instrument played by striking the strings with a pair of light wooden mallets.

• He was awarded the Padma Shri (1991) and Padma Vibhushan (2001), and with Hariprasad Chaurasia composed music as the duo 'Shiv-Hari' (films *Silsila*, *Chandni*, *Lamhe*).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Ustad Amjad Ali Khan — Sarod (Bangash gharana), Padma Vibhushan.

• Ustad Zakir Hussain — Tabla, son of Ustad Alla Rakha; Padma Vibhushan and Grammy winner.

• Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia — Bansuri (flute), Padma Vibhushan.

NOTE

• Instrument–artist pairs: Sitar — Pt. Ravi Shankar, Ustad Vilayat Khan; Sarangi — Pt. Ram Narayan; Shehnai — Ustad Bismillah Khan; Veena — S. Balachander; Mandolin — U. Srinivas; Violin — Dr. L. Subramaniam.

• Classification of Indian instruments: Tata (string), Sushira (wind), Avanaddha (membrane/percussion), Ghana (solid/idiophone).

question: Under the Delhi Sultanate, a religious tax ______ was imposed on the wealthy and rich Muslims in India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Zakat.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Zakat was a religious tax collected only from wealthy Muslims, generally at the rate of 2.5% of their property/wealth, and was spent on the welfare of the Muslim community. (जकात)

• It was one of the four main taxes of the Delhi Sultanate sanctioned by Islamic law, along with Kharaj, Jizya and Khams.

• Firoz Shah Tughlaq declared that he levied only these four taxes and abolished 23 other cesses (abwabs); he also imposed a separate irrigation tax called Haqq-i-Sharb.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Kharaj — the land tax paid by non-Muslim cultivators, usually one-third to one-half of the produce (raised to 50% by Alauddin Khalji).

• Jizya — a religious tax on non-Muslims in return for protection; abolished by Akbar in 1564 and re-imposed by Aurangzeb in 1679.

• Khams — the state's share (1/5th, raised to 4/5th by Alauddin Khalji) of war booty.

• 'Firuz' was a Sultan and 'Mamluk' (Slave dynasty, 1206–1290) was a dynasty — neither is a tax.

NOTE

• Alauddin Khalji introduced market (price) control measures and the Diwan-i-Riyasat; he also began the practice of measurement of land (masahat).

• Delhi Sultanate dynasties in order: Slave/Mamluk (1206) → Khalji (1290) → Tughlaq (1320) → Sayyid (1414) → Lodi (1451–1526).

question: How many silver medals won by India in Commonwealth Games 2022?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 16.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• At the Commonwealth Games 2022 held at Birmingham, England (28 July – 8 August 2022), India won a total of 61 medals — 22 gold, 16 silver and 23 bronze. (राष्ट्रमंडल खेल)

• India finished 4th in the medal tally, behind Australia, England and Canada.

• India's flag-bearers at the opening ceremony were P. V. Sindhu and Manpreet Singh; Achanta Sharath Kamal was the flag-bearer at the closing ceremony and won 3 gold + 1 silver.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• India's best-ever CWG performance was at Delhi 2010 — 101 medals (38 gold), finishing 2nd.

• Wrestling gave India the most medals in 2022 (12 — 6 gold, 1 silver, 5 bronze); weightlifting gave 10.

• Mirabai Chanu won gold in weightlifting (49 kg) and Nikhat Zareen in boxing.

NOTE

• The 2022 CWG mascot was 'Perry the Bull'; motto — 'Games for Everyone'.

• The 2026 Commonwealth Games are to be held in Glasgow, Scotland; the 2018 edition was at Gold Coast, Australia.

question: The term 'Kammakaras' in ancient times is related to ________ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Landless agricultural labourers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In ancient Indian (Buddhist/Pali) texts, 'Kammakaras' referred to landless agricultural labourers who worked for wages on the fields of others. (भूमिहीन कृषि मजदूर)

• They belonged to the lower strata of society in the 6th century BCE, along with the dasas (slaves), and are frequently mentioned in Pali literature dealing with the Mahajanapada period.

• The landowning peasants of the time were called gahapatis, while large landowners were known as grihapatis/setthi-gahapatis.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Craftsmen and artisans organised themselves into guilds called shrenis; the head of a guild was the jetthaka/pramukha.

• Tax collecting officers in ancient India included the Bhaga-dugha (Vedic), Samaharta (chief revenue collector) and Sannidhata (treasurer) of the Mauryan administration described in Kautilya's Arthashastra.

• The term for the land revenue collected in ancient times was bhaga, usually 1/6th of the produce — hence the king was called shadbhagin.

NOTE

• Other terms: Dasa — slave; Gahapati — householder/landowner; Setthi — rich merchant/banker; Sarthavaha — caravan trader.

• The 16 Mahajanapadas are listed in the Buddhist text Anguttara Nikaya; Magadha became the most powerful of them.

question: Which among the following parts of the Indian Constitution deals with 'The Panchayats'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is IX.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) of the Constitution, titled 'The Panchayats', was inserted by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (came into force 24 April 1993). (पंचायत)

• It gives constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions and adds the Eleventh Schedule, listing 29 functional items of the panchayats.

• It provides for a three-tier system (Village, Intermediate and District level), a five-year term, reservation of 1/3rd seats for women and seats for SC/ST, and a State Election Commission and State Finance Commission.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Part IXA (Articles 243P–243ZG) — 'The Municipalities', added by the 74th Amendment Act, 1992, with the Twelfth Schedule (18 items).

• Part III (Articles 12–35) — Fundamental Rights; Part IV — DPSP; Part VI (Articles 152–237) — the States.

• Part X (Articles 244–244A) — the Scheduled and Tribal Areas.

NOTE

• The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj; Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959) was the first state to implement it, followed by Andhra Pradesh.

• Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system; L. M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommended constitutional status for panchayats.

• National Panchayati Raj Day is observed on 24 April.

question: The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Bill, 2021 is related to ____ Ministry of India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Environment, Forests & Climate Change.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Bill, 2021 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 December 2021 by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). (पर्यावरण, वन एवं जलवायु परिवर्तन मंत्रालय)

• It amends the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, which was enacted to give effect to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), 1992.

• Aims: to encourage Indian systems of medicine (AYUSH), promote cultivation of medicinal plants, ease compliance for domestic companies, and decriminalise offences (penalties instead of imprisonment).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The parent Act created a three-tier structure: the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA, Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards, and Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at the local level.

• Other MoEFCC laws: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Water Act, 1974, Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

• The Bill was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee and was passed as the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023.

NOTE

• CBD was adopted at the Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro, 1992; its supplementary protocols are the Cartagena Protocol (2000, biosafety) and the Nagoya Protocol (2010, access and benefit sharing).

• India is one of the 17 megadiverse countries; it has 4 biodiversity hotspots — Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar).

question:
Which of the following is an important steel producing centres in India?

I. Bhilai

II. Jamshedpur

III. Rourkela
solution_text:
The correct answer is I, II and III.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• All three — Bhilai, Jamshedpur and Rourkela — are major iron and steel producing centres of India, all located in the mineral-rich Chhota Nagpur plateau belt of eastern-central India. (लौह-इस्पात केंद्र)

• Bhilai (Chhattisgarh) — set up in 1955 with Russian (USSR) collaboration; iron ore comes from Dalli-Rajhara.

• Jamshedpur (Jharkhand) — TISCO, established in 1907 by Jamsetji Tata on the Subarnarekha river; India's first modern integrated steel plant.

• Rourkela (Odisha) — set up in 1959 with German collaboration, on the Brahmani river; iron ore from Sundargarh/Keonjhar.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Durgapur (West Bengal) — British collaboration; Bokaro (Jharkhand) — Russian collaboration (1964).

• Later plants: Salem (Tamil Nadu), Vijayanagar/Bhadravati (Karnataka) and Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) — the only port-based steel plant.

• India is the world's second largest crude steel producer after China.

NOTE

• Requirements of the iron-and-steel industry: iron ore, coking coal, limestone, manganese, water and cheap transport — hence plants cluster in the Chhota Nagpur plateau.

• SAIL manages Bhilai, Durgapur, Rourkela, Bokaro and IISCO-Burnpur.

question: Which freedom fighter is known as the mother of the Indian revolution?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madam Bhikaji Cama.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Madam Bhikaji Rustom Cama (1861–1936) is known as the 'Mother of the Indian Revolution'. (भारतीय क्रांति की माता)

• On 22 August 1907 she unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag on foreign soil at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany.

• She worked from abroad (Paris and London) with revolutionaries such as Shyamji Krishna Varma and Veer Savarkar, and helped publish the journal 'Bande Mataram' from Paris.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Sarojini Naidu — the 'Nightingale of India' (Bharat Kokila); first Indian woman President of the INC (Kanpur, 1925) and first woman Governor (United Provinces).

• Annie Besant — founded the Home Rule League (1916) at Madras, first woman President of the INC (Calcutta, 1917), and edited 'New India' and 'Commonweal'.

• Aruna Asaf Ali — the 'Grand Old Lady of the Independence Movement', who hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank, Bombay during the Quit India Movement, 1942.

NOTE

• Other titles: Matangini Hazra — 'Gandhi Buri'; Rani Gaidinliu — 'Rani of the Nagas'; Kittur Rani Chennamma — early woman ruler to fight the British (1824).

• The first President of the INC (1885) was W. C. Bonnerjee; the first woman was Annie Besant.

question: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) is regulated by _________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Reserve Bank of India.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) is an All-India Financial Institution (AIFI) and, like other AIFIs, it is regulated and supervised by the Reserve Bank of India. (भारतीय लघु उद्योग विकास बैंक)

• It was set up on 2 April 1990 under an Act of Parliament (SIDBI Act, 1989) as the principal financial institution for the promotion, financing and development of the MSME sector.

• Its headquarters is at Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. It was originally a wholly-owned subsidiary of IDBI.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The other AIFIs regulated by the RBI are NABARD (1982, Mumbai), EXIM Bank (1982, Mumbai), NHB (1988, New Delhi) and NaBFID (2021).

• SBI is India's largest commercial bank (established as Imperial Bank in 1921; renamed SBI on 1 July 1955) and ICICI Bank and Indian Bank are ordinary commercial banks — none of them regulates SIDBI.

• SIDBI runs schemes such as Udyami Mitra portal, Stand-Up India, CGTMSE and the Fund of Funds for Startups.

NOTE

• The RBI was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission, and was nationalised on 1 January 1949.

• MSME classification (2020): Micro — investment ≤ ₹1 cr & turnover ≤ ₹5 cr; Small — ≤ ₹10 cr & ≤ ₹50 cr; Medium — ≤ ₹50 cr & ≤ ₹250 cr.

question: Which of the following states does NOT share border with Nepal?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Himachal Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Five Indian states share a border with Nepal — Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim. (नेपाल की सीमा)

• Himachal Pradesh does NOT touch Nepal; it shares an international border only with China (Tibet).

• The India–Nepal border is about 1,751 km long and is an open border; it is guarded by the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Nepal is a landlocked Himalayan country; capital Kathmandu, currency Nepalese rupee.

• Kalapani, Limpiyadhura and Lipulekh are the disputed areas between India and Nepal in Uttarakhand.

• Himachal Pradesh borders Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand and Tibet (China).

NOTE

• Indian states bordering China: Ladakh (UT), Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.

• States bordering Bhutan: Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh; Bangladesh: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

• West Bengal and Sikkim are the only states that touch Nepal in the east; West Bengal touches the most countries (Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh).

question: Provisions related to the Municipalities are mentioned under which part of the Indian constitution?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Part IXA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part IXA (Articles 243P to 243ZG), titled 'The Municipalities', was inserted by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which came into force on 1 June 1993. (नगरपालिकाएँ)

• It also added the Twelfth Schedule, which lists 18 functional items of the municipalities (urban planning, water supply, slum improvement, public health, etc.).

• It provides for three types of urban bodies — Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area) and Municipal Corporation (larger urban area).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Part IX — 'The Panchayats' (73rd Amendment, 1992) with the Eleventh Schedule (29 items).

• Part V (Articles 52–151) — the Union; Part VI (152–237) — the States; Part VII dealt with Part B States and was repealed by the 7th Amendment Act, 1956.

• Part XII (Articles 264–300A) — Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits.

NOTE

• Municipal bodies must have a five-year term, 1/3rd reservation for women and reservation for SC/ST in proportion to population.

• India's first municipal corporation was set up at Madras (Chennai) in 1688; Lord Ripon (1882) is called the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India'.

question: Which among the following plant kingdoms are divided into dicotyledons and monocotyledons?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Angiosperms.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Angiosperms (flowering plants, seeds enclosed inside a fruit) are divided into two classes on the basis of the number of cotyledons (seed leaves) in the seed — Monocotyledons (one cotyledon) and Dicotyledons (two cotyledons). (आवृतबीजी)

• Monocots: parallel venation, fibrous roots, trimerous flowers — e.g., wheat, rice, maize, grass, onion.

• Dicots: reticulate venation, tap root, tetramerous/pentamerous flowers — e.g., gram, pea, mango, mustard, neem.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Gymnosperms — naked-seeded plants with no fruit or ovary; e.g., Pinus, Cycas, Cedrus.

• Pteridophytes — the first vascular land plants (tracheophytes); e.g., ferns, Marsilea, Equisetum; they reproduce by spores.

• Bryophytes — the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom', non-vascular; e.g., mosses, Riccia, Marchantia.

NOTE

• Plant kingdom classification (Eichler): Thallophyta → Bryophyta → Pteridophyta → Gymnosperms → Angiosperms.

• Carolus Linnaeus is called the Father of Taxonomy and gave binomial nomenclature; his work *Species Plantarum* (1753) named plants.

question: Which among the following type of unemployment is also known as the real wage unemployment?
solution_text:
The correct answer is classical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Classical unemployment is also called real-wage unemployment. It occurs when real wages are kept above the market-clearing (equilibrium) level, so that the supply of labour exceeds the demand for labour. (शास्त्रीय/वास्तविक मजदूरी बेरोजगारी)

• It usually results from minimum wage laws, trade-union pressure or wage rigidity, which prevent wages from falling to the equilibrium level.

• Classical economists held that unemployment would disappear on its own if wages were allowed to fall freely — a view challenged by J. M. Keynes.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Seasonal unemployment — occurs only in certain seasons; common in agriculture, ice-cream and tourism industries.

• Structural unemployment — arises from a mismatch between workers' skills and the jobs available due to changes in technology or the structure of the economy.

• Frictional (search) unemployment — the temporary unemployment while a person moves between jobs; it is short-term and unavoidable.

NOTE

• Disguised unemployment — more people are employed than actually needed (marginal productivity is zero); typical of Indian agriculture.

• Cyclical unemployment — caused by a downturn in the business cycle/recession; Educated unemployment — qualified persons unable to find suitable jobs.

• Unemployment data in India is collected through the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) by the NSO, started in 2017.

question: Nalanda University, an important learning centre in ancient period is situated in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bihar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Nalanda Mahavihara, the great Buddhist residential university of ancient India, is situated in the present-day Nalanda district of Bihar, near Rajgir. (नालंदा)

• It was founded in the 5th century CE by Kumaragupta I of the Gupta dynasty and was patronised later by Harshavardhana and the Pala rulers.

• The Chinese travellers Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) and I-Tsing studied here in the 7th century. It was destroyed around 1193 CE by Bakhtiyar Khalji.

• Nalanda Mahavihara was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Other ancient centres of learning: Vikramshila and Odantapuri (Bihar), Takshashila (now in Pakistan), Valabhi (Gujarat), Somapura (Bangladesh) and Kanchipuram (Tamil Nadu).

• Vikramshila University was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala.

• A modern Nalanda University was re-established at Rajgir under the Nalanda University Act, 2010.

NOTE

• Bihar's capital is Patna (ancient Pataliputra), the capital of the Magadha, Maurya and Gupta empires.

• Other Bihar sites: Bodh Gaya (enlightenment of Buddha), Rajgir, Vaishali (first republic; Buddha's last sermon), Pawapuri (nirvana of Mahavira).

question: Who among the following won the Men's Singles Paris Masters Title in 2022?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Holger Rune.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Holger Rune of Denmark won the men's singles title at the Paris Masters (Rolex Paris Masters) 2022, defeating Novak Djokovic in the final by 3–6, 6–3, 7–5. (पेरिस मास्टर्स)

• It was Rune's first ATP Masters 1000 title; he was then only 19 years old and became the first player to beat five top-10 opponents on the way to a Masters 1000 title.

• The Paris Masters is an indoor hard-court ATP Masters 1000 event held in Paris, France, and is the last Masters 1000 event of the season.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Carlos Alcaraz (Spain) won the US Open 2022 and finished 2022 as the youngest year-end World No. 1 in ATP history.

• Novak Djokovic (Serbia) won Wimbledon 2022 and the ATP Finals 2022 (held at Turin).

• Casper Ruud (Norway) was the runner-up at both the French Open 2022 and the US Open 2022.

NOTE

• The four Grand Slams: Australian Open (hard), French Open/Roland Garros (clay), Wimbledon (grass) and US Open (hard).

• 2022 Grand Slam men's singles winners: Rafael Nadal (Australian Open and French Open), Novak Djokovic (Wimbledon), Carlos Alcaraz (US Open).

question: Which former Miss India, also the recipient of the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, popularised Indian classical dance in the west?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indrani Rahman.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Indrani Rahman (1930–1999) won the Miss India title in 1952 and became one of the earliest Indian dancers to popularise Indian classical dance in the West. (इंद्राणी रहमान)

• She was an accomplished exponent of Bharatanatyam, Odissi, Kuchipudi and Kathakali, and was among the first to take Odissi to national and international audiences.

• She received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1969) and the Padma Shri (1969). She later settled in New York and taught at the Juilliard School.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Her mother, Ragini Devi (Esther Sherman), an American, was herself a pioneer of Indian classical dance revival.

• Leela Naidu was a famous actress and one of the winners of an early Miss India contest, but she is known for cinema (*Anuradha*, *The Householder*), not classical dance.

• The Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's national academy for music, dance and drama, was set up in 1953.

NOTE

• India's 8 classical dances: Bharatanatyam (TN), Kathak (UP), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (AP), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• Famous exponents: Rukmini Devi Arundale and Balasaraswati (Bharatanatyam), Birju Maharaj (Kathak), Kelucharan Mohapatra (Odissi).
